---
title: "Choose a format"
description: "Compare Frame Job's fifteen export formats and pick the one that suits where the file is going."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

The **Format:** popup in the [export sheet](/export/export-sheet/) decides the codec and the container together. Pick it by where the file is going next.

<AtAGlance
  where="Export sheet ▸ Format"
  tools="export"
/>

## Pick by what the file is for

| You want | Choose |
| --- | --- |
| A file every player and upload form takes | [H.264 (MP4)](/export/h264-and-hevc/#h264-mp4), the default |
| A smaller file at the same picture | [HEVC (MP4)](/export/h264-and-hevc/#hevc-mp4) |
| The smallest delivery file, and time to spare | [AV1 (MP4)](/export/av1-and-vp9/#av1-mp4) |
| To keep a 10-bit source's gradients in a delivery file | [HEVC 10-bit (MP4)](/export/h264-and-hevc/#hevc-10-bit-mp4) |
| A movie for a web page | [VP9 (WebM)](/export/av1-and-vp9/#vp9-webm) or [AV1 (WebM)](/export/av1-and-vp9/#av1-webm) |
| A master for another editing application | [ProRes 422 (MOV)](/export/prores/#prores-422-mov) |
| A title or lower third with transparency | [ProRes 4444 (MOV)](/export/prores/#prores-4444-mov) as a master, [HEVC with Alpha (MOV)](/export/h264-and-hevc/#hevc-with-alpha-mov) for Safari and Apple's apps, or [VP9 with Alpha (WebM)](/export/av1-and-vp9/#vp9-with-alpha-webm) for Chrome and Firefox |
| Sound and no picture | [An audio-only format](/export/audio-only/) |
| A short silent loop | [Animated GIF or Animated PNG](/export/gif-and-apng/) |

## The formats

They're listed in the popup's order.

| Format | What it's for | File | Sound | Picture depth | Keeps transparency | Can carry HDR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H.264 (MP4) | The everyday delivery file | `.mp4` | AAC | 8-bit | No | No |
| HEVC (MP4) | A smaller file at the same picture | `.mp4` | AAC | 8-bit | No | No |
| HEVC with Alpha (MOV) | A small transparent delivery file | `.mov` | AAC | 8-bit | Yes | No |
| HEVC 10-bit (MP4) | Keeps a 10-bit source's gradients | `.mp4` | AAC | 10-bit | No | Yes |
| AV1 (MP4) | The smallest delivery file | `.mp4` | AAC | 10-bit | No | Yes |
| AV1 (WebM) | The same AV1 picture, for the web | `.webm` | Opus | 10-bit | No | Yes |
| VP9 (WebM) | The web format every browser plays | `.webm` | Opus | 8-bit, or 10-bit when it carries HDR | No | Yes |
| VP9 with Alpha (WebM) | A transparent movie for Chrome and Firefox | `.webm` | Opus | 8-bit | Yes | No |
| ProRes 422 (MOV) | An editing master for another application | `.mov` | 16-bit LPCM | 10-bit | No | Yes |
| ProRes 4444 (MOV) | A master that keeps transparency | `.mov` | 16-bit LPCM | 12-bit | Yes | Yes |
| Audio only (M4A) | Compressed sound to send | `.m4a` | AAC | None | None | None |
| Audio only (WAV) | Uncompressed sound for another tool | `.wav` | 16-bit or 24-bit LPCM | None | None | None |
| Audio only (AIFF) | The same samples as WAV, in an AIFF | `.aiff` | 16-bit or 24-bit LPCM | None | None | None |
| Animated GIF | A short silent loop to send | `.gif` | None | 8-bit, 256 colours | No | No |
| Animated PNG | A lossless silent loop | `.png` | None | 8-bit | Yes | No |

In an HDR project, a video format that can't carry HDR writes the project's SDR version. See [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/). On a transparent canvas, a format that doesn't keep transparency composites the picture onto black, and a GIF has a rule of its own. See [Transparent exports](/export/transparency/).

## Sound in each format

Every file with sound is stereo at 48 kHz.

| Sound | Formats |
| --- | --- |
| AAC | H.264, HEVC, HEVC with Alpha, HEVC 10-bit, AV1 (MP4) and M4A |
| Opus | AV1 (WebM), VP9 (WebM) and VP9 with Alpha (WebM) |
| 16-bit LPCM | ProRes 422 and ProRes 4444 |
| 16-bit or 24-bit LPCM | WAV and AIFF. See [Export bit depth](/export/bit-depth/). |
| None | GIF and APNG |

AAC and Opus run at 192 kbps unless a [Quality tier](/export/quality/) says otherwise.

A file's sound is as long as the range it exports, including when a clip in it plays faster or slower. A project with no sound exports a movie with no sound track, in a WebM as in any other movie format.

## Changing the format

Changing the format rebuilds the **Size:** list and returns it to that format's default, because a GIF's default isn't an H.264's. Your frame rate, quality, loudness and range choices stay as they were, whether or not the new format can use them.

Picking the format that's already chosen changes nothing, so a custom size you've typed survives it.

## Software and hardware encoders

AV1 and VP9 are encoded in software, by encoders built into Frame Job, so they take longer than the HEVC formats, which use the Mac's hardware encoder. The sheet [estimates the time](/export/export-sheet/#estimated-time) for AV1 and VP9, and AV1's [**Speed:** row](/export/encoder-speed/) trades time against file size.

## No encoder

A Mac with no encoder for a format reports it and leaves no file. The message names the format by its short name, for example: "This Mac cannot export with the “hevc_alpha” preset."

## Related

- [The export sheet](/export/export-sheet/)
- [Export quality](/export/quality/)
- [Export size](/export/size/)
- [Transparent exports](/export/transparency/)

---
title: "H.264 and HEVC"
description: "Know what the H.264, HEVC, HEVC 10-bit and HEVC with Alpha formats write, and which one suits your delivery file."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

These four formats are for delivery. H.264 is the file everything takes, HEVC is smaller, HEVC 10-bit keeps a deep source's gradients, and HEVC with Alpha keeps a transparent canvas.

<AtAGlance
  where="Export sheet ▸ Format"
  tools="export"
/>

| Format | File | Picture | Keeps transparency | In an HDR project | Rate at 1080p, 30 fps with Format default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [H.264 (MP4)](#h264-mp4) | `.mp4` | 8-bit | No | Writes the SDR version | About 8.7 Mbps |
| [HEVC (MP4)](#hevc-mp4) | `.mp4` | 8-bit | No | Writes the SDR version | About 4.4 Mbps |
| [HEVC 10-bit (MP4)](#hevc-10-bit-mp4) | `.mp4` | 10-bit | No | Writes HDR | About 4.4 Mbps |
| [HEVC with Alpha (MOV)](#hevc-with-alpha-mov) | `.mov` | 8-bit | Yes | Writes the SDR version | About 4.4 Mbps |

All four share these:

- A keyframe at least every 2 seconds, so the file scrubs and re-cuts well.
- AAC sound, stereo at 48 kHz, at 192 kbps unless a [Quality tier](/export/quality/) says otherwise.
- Even dimensions. An odd width or height is written one pixel smaller. See [Export size](/export/size/).
- [Chapters](/export/chapters/) from your chapter markers.

## H.264 (MP4)

This is the default, the first row of the **Format:** popup, so <kbd>⌘E</kbd> writes it unless you've chosen otherwise. Every player and upload form takes it.

It writes 8-bit video in the High profile. With **Format default**, the rate follows the frame at 0.14 bits per pixel per frame, held between 1 and 200 Mbps.

H.264 has no alpha channel, so a transparent canvas is flattened onto black.

## HEVC (MP4)

HEVC gives you the same picture in about half the rate of H.264, though not everything accepts it yet. It uses the Mac's hardware encoder.

It writes 8-bit video in the Main profile, even from a deep source. With **Format default**, the rate is 0.07 bits per pixel per frame, held between 1 and 200 Mbps. The Quality tiers ask for 60 % of H.264's rate.

## HEVC 10-bit (MP4)

HEVC 10-bit writes HEVC's Main 10 profile from Frame Job's deep frames, so a 10-bit source keeps its gradients in a delivery file. Its rates are HEVC's.

It's one of the six formats that can carry HDR. In an HLG project it writes HLG unless you change **Dynamic Range:**, and no Dolby Vision is added to the file. See [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/).

## HEVC with Alpha (MOV)

This is a small delivery movie that keeps a transparent canvas, for laying over another background. It's the transparent movie for Safari, QuickTime and Apple's apps. For a web page in Chrome or Firefox, see [VP9 with Alpha (WebM)](/export/av1-and-vp9/#vp9-with-alpha-webm), and for a master, [ProRes 4444 (MOV)](/export/prores/#prores-4444-mov).

- It's a `.mov` because this codec can't be written into an `.mp4`.
- The picture and its alpha are both 8-bit, and the colour is straight, not multiplied by the transparency.
- It takes HEVC's rates and Quality tiers, and the [footnote](/export/export-sheet/#the-footnote) ends in `alpha`.
- [Fast start](#fast-start) is off.

Every row in the **Size:** popup has the canvas's shape, so those are all fine. A **Custom…** size of a different shape won't export, because padding it would lose the alpha. After the save panel the export stops with a message naming the canvas's size. A size within a pixel of the canvas's shape, or in the same proportions at any scale, is fine.

## Fast start

MP4 and M4A files are written with their index at the front, so a player can start before the whole file has downloaded. There's no control for this in the sheet.

Fast start is on for MP4 and M4A, and off for MOV, WAV, AIFF, GIF and APNG. A WebM's index is at the front anyway.

## Good to know

H.264, HEVC and HEVC with Alpha are all 8-bit, so in an HDR project they write the project's SDR version and **Dynamic Range:** stays greyed out on **SDR version**. To deliver HDR in this family, use HEVC 10-bit.

## Related

- [Choose a format](/export/formats/)
- [Export quality](/export/quality/)
- [Transparent exports](/export/transparency/)
- [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/)

---
title: "AV1 and VP9"
description: "Export small delivery files and web movies with Frame Job's built-in AV1 and VP9 encoders, and know how their rates, time and memory behave."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

AV1 and VP9 are the formats for the smallest delivery files and for the web. Frame Job has their encoders built in, SVT-AV1 and libvpx, and they run in software, so they take longer than HEVC.

<AtAGlance
  where={['Export sheet ▸ Format', 'Export sheet ▸ Speed (AV1 only)']}
  tools="export"
/>

| Format | File | Sound | Picture | Keeps transparency | Can carry HDR | **Speed:** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [AV1 (MP4)](#av1-mp4) | `.mp4` | AAC | 10-bit | No | Yes | Yes |
| [AV1 (WebM)](#av1-webm) | `.webm` | Opus | 10-bit | No | Yes | Yes |
| [VP9 (WebM)](#vp9-webm) | `.webm` | Opus | 8-bit, or 10-bit with HDR | No | Yes | Greyed out |
| [VP9 with Alpha (WebM)](#vp9-with-alpha-webm) | `.webm` | Opus | 8-bit | Yes | No | Greyed out |

All four write a keyframe at least every 2 seconds and need even dimensions, so an odd width or height is written one pixel smaller. All four write [chapters](/export/chapters/). The sheet [estimates the time](/export/export-sheet/#estimated-time) before you start.

## AV1 (MP4)

This is the smallest delivery file: AV1 video and AAC sound in an MP4. It's always 10-bit.

**Speed:** offers **Faster**, **Balanced** and **Smaller file**, with **Balanced** the default. See [Encoder speed](/export/encoder-speed/). Slower settings take longer and write a smaller file.

It encodes at a constant quality matched to HEVC, with the rate as a [soft cap](#the-rate-as-a-soft-cap). It's one of the six formats that can carry HDR. See [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/).

An M1 or M2 Mac can't [play the file back](#playback-on-m1-and-m2-macs).

## AV1 (WebM)

The same AV1 picture in a WebM file, for the web. It has the same encoder, speeds, soft cap and HDR as AV1 (MP4). Only the container and the sound differ.

The sound is Opus, 48 kHz stereo, at 192 kbps unless a [Quality tier](/export/quality/) says otherwise, and it snaps to the nearest rate the encoder offers. A project with no sound exports a WebM with no sound track.

## VP9 (WebM)

VP9 in a WebM file with Opus sound: the web format every browser plays. It's larger than AV1 for the same picture and slower to export than HEVC. It has one speed, so **Speed:** is greyed out.

An SDR picture is 8-bit, in VP9's Profile 0, which every player decodes. HDR is 10-bit, in Profile 2. VP9 can't name HLG or PQ itself, so the WebM file tells the player which one it is. See [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/).

## VP9 with Alpha (WebM)

VP9 (WebM) that keeps a transparent canvas, for a title or lower third a web page plays over its own background in Chrome or Firefox. It's a Safari-free choice: Safari hasn't been confirmed to show its transparency, and Safari's transparent movie is [HEVC with Alpha (MOV)](/export/h264-and-hevc/#hevc-with-alpha-mov). Only a player that decodes VP9 with libvpx shows the transparency, and others show the picture opaque.

- The picture is 8-bit, with the transparency as a second stream beside it. The [footnote](/export/export-sheet/#the-footnote) ends in `alpha`.
- It's SDR only, so an HDR project writes its SDR version, and **Dynamic Range:** stays greyed out on **SDR version**.
- The sound is Opus, as in VP9 (WebM).
- A **Custom…** size of a different shape from the canvas won't export, because padding would lose the alpha. After the save panel the export stops with a message naming the canvas's size. Every row in the **Size:** popup is fine.
- Imported back into Frame Job it shows opaque, with black where it was transparent. For a transparent clip to bring back in, export ProRes 4444 or HEVC with Alpha.

## The rate as a soft cap

On AV1 and VP9 the video rate isn't a target. They encode at a constant quality chosen to match or beat HEVC at that rate, and the file usually stays under it. That's why the Quality tiers and the footnote read `usually ≤ …`.

- With **Format default** the cap is HEVC's rate. With a tier it's 60 % of the H.264 rate, as for HEVC. See [Export quality](/export/quality/).
- Simple footage comes out much smaller than the rate.
- Very detailed footage can go over it: up to about 1.25 times on AV1, and about 1.15 times on VP9.
- In an HDR export, VP9 matches HEVC 10-bit at that rate.
- You can't know the file size in advance.

On VP9 with Alpha the rate is the picture's alone. The transparency is a second stream at a fixed quality on top of it, so the file is larger than the rate says. On a moving soft-edged shape, the transparency measured about 6 to 15 % of the video at 1080p, 9 to 21 % at 720p, and 21 to 39 % at 640 × 360, with the higher figures at the Low tier.

## Memory and the queue

These encoders use far more memory than the Mac's own. A job in the [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) waits while the AV1 and VP9 exports already running would use more than a quarter of the Mac's memory with it. Its row says why, for example "Waiting for memory: AV1 and VP9 exports running now hold about 6.0 GB of the 8.0 GB this Mac allows them, and this one needs about 3.0 GB." A later job may run first meanwhile.

A job always starts when no other AV1 or VP9 export is running. **Export…** never waits, so starting several at once behind their progress sheets can go past that quarter. The memory each job needs is a measured figure, not a guarantee, and a heavier timeline can use more.

## Playback on M1 and M2 Macs

M1 and M2 Macs have no AV1 decoder, so neither Frame Job nor QuickTime can play or re-import an AV1 file there, MP4 or WebM. The Mac can still export one.

A VP9 (WebM) file re-imports on any Apple silicon Mac.

## Good to know

An AV1 rate is held at 100 Mbps at most, whatever a tier works out to at a very large size.

## Related

- [Encoder speed](/export/encoder-speed/)
- [Export quality](/export/quality/)
- [Transparent exports](/export/transparency/)
- [The Export Queue](/export/export-queue/)

---
title: "Animated GIF and PNG"
description: "Export a short silent loop as an Animated GIF or Animated PNG, and keep it inside the size and the 600-frame limit."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

GIF and APNG are for short silent loops you can send or drop into a page. Each stores every frame as a whole picture, so a long or large one quickly becomes a file nobody can send. That's why both start small and hold at most 600 frames.

<AtAGlance
  where="Export sheet ▸ Format"
  tools="export"
/>

## Export a loop

<Steps>

1. Set an [in/out range](/timeline/in-out-range/) around the moment you want.

2. Press <kbd>⌘E</kbd>, and choose **Animated GIF** or **Animated PNG** from **Format:**.

3. Set **Range:** to **In/out range**.

4. Check the readout, which shows the size and the frame count, such as `· 360 frames, no audio`.

5. Choose **Export…**.

</Steps>

## Animated GIF

A GIF is a short, silent `.gif` that loops forever. It starts at 480 × 270 and 12.5 fps, and you can still change the size and the rate.

The 12.5 is deliberate. A GIF stores each frame's delay in hundredths of a second, so only rates that divide 100 play back exactly. 25 and 50 fps from the **Frame rate:** popup do too, and any other rate lands wherever the format's rounding puts it.

A GIF has a palette of 256 colours. It can show a pixel as fully transparent but has no partial transparency, so soft edges go hard, and it isn't one of the [formats that keep transparency](/export/transparency/).

## Animated PNG

An APNG is a lossless, silent, true-colour `.png` that loops forever. It starts at 960 × 540 and 25 fps, and you can still change the size and the rate.

It keeps real transparency, so a pixel can be any fraction of opaque, and the [footnote](/export/export-sheet/#the-footnote) ends in `alpha`. It's written at 8 bits a component and labelled BT.709.

A viewer that knows nothing of APNG shows the first frame.

## The 600-frame limit

An animated GIF or APNG holds at most 600 frames. That's 48 seconds at GIF's 12.5 fps, or 24 seconds at APNG's 25 fps. The readout shows the count while you're choosing, but the sheet doesn't stop you. Once you've picked where to save, a longer export stops before it writes anything:

> An animated GIF is limited to 600 frames and this range is 720. Shorten the range, or lower the export frame rate.

For GIF the way out is a shorter range, because every fixed rate in the **Frame rate:** popup is higher than 12.5 fps. An APNG can go down to 24 or 23.976 fps, which gains you about a second.

## Fitting inside the size

The **Size:** popup lists **GIF default** or **APNG default** first, and it's the default for those two formats and no others. Each is 480 × 270 or 960 × 540, fitted to the canvas's shape.

Every row, and a **Custom…** size, is a box the picture fits inside. It keeps its shape and is never enlarged, and nothing is letterboxed. The rows show the size the file will have. A 1080 × 1920 project's GIF default is 152 × 270.

Because the picture is never enlarged, rows bigger than the canvas come out as the canvas's own size, and the popup hides rows that repeat an earlier row's numbers. An odd width or height is kept.

## Good to know

- **Quality:** and **Loudness:** are greyed out, and so are **Bit depth:** and **Stems:**. Neither format has a bit rate or any sound.
- **Burn in timecode** still works.
- Neither format has [chapters](/export/chapters/).
- Both write the SDR version in an HDR project.

## Related

- [Choose a format](/export/formats/)
- [Export a range](/export/range/)
- [Export size](/export/size/)
- [Export frame rate](/export/frame-rate/)

---
title: "The export sheet"
description: "Choose a format and its settings, see what the file will be before anything is written, then export now or add the job to the queue."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

One sheet turns the timeline into a movie, an audio file or an animated image. It shows you the size, rate, length and codec of the file before anything is written.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ Export…"
  keys="⌘E"
  where="The accent Export… button at the right end of the toolbar"
  tools={['export', 'export_status', 'cancel_export']}
/>

## Open the export sheet

<Steps>

1. Choose **File ▸ Export…**, press <kbd>⌘E</kbd>, or click **Export…** at the right end of the toolbar. Playback pauses and the sheet opens over the editor window.

2. Choose a [format](/export/formats/), then change whichever other controls you need.

3. Read the [readout line](#the-readout-line) and the [footnote](#the-footnote) under the controls. They say what the file will be.

4. Choose [**Export…** or **Add to Queue**](#export-or-add-to-queue), then pick where to save the file.

</Steps>

While the timeline is empty, **File ▸ Export…** is greyed out and there's no sheet to open. A timeline of nothing but text, shapes, images and graphics still exports. You can't edit the project while the sheet is open.

An export always writes the whole timeline, even when you're working inside a [nest](/editing/nests/).

<Shot
  name="12-export-sheet.sheet"
  alt="The Export sheet with a paragraph of help under its title, then the controls: Preset on Custom, Format on H.264 (MP4), Speed greyed on Balanced, Size on Document size 960 × 540 with two greyed fields, Frame rate on Project rate, Quality on Format default, Bit depth greyed on 16-bit, Stems greyed on None, Loudness on Off, Range greyed on Whole project, and an unticked Burn in timecode. Below them the readout reads 960 × 540, 30 fps, 00:00:05:07, the footnote reads H264, MP4, and the buttons are Add to Queue, Cancel and Export…."

## The controls

From top to bottom:

| Control | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Preset:** | Applies a set of choices you saved. The gear beside it saves and deletes them. See [Export presets](/export/presets/). | Custom |
| **Format:** | The encoding, a container and a codec together. See [Choose a format](/export/formats/). | H.264 (MP4) |
| **Dynamic Range:** | Which picture an HDR project writes. The row is there only in an HLG project. See [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/). | HDR (HLG) |
| **Speed:** | How long the AV1 encoder works on each frame. See [Encoder speed](/export/encoder-speed/). | Balanced |
| **Size:** | The frame size, or **Custom…** with width and height fields on the row below. See [Export size](/export/size/). | The format's first row |
| **Frame rate:** | **Project rate**, or a fixed rate. See [Export frame rate](/export/frame-rate/). | Project rate |
| **Quality:** | **Format default**, or a bit-rate tier. See [Export quality](/export/quality/). | Format default |
| **Bit depth:** | **16-bit** or **24-bit**, for a WAV or an AIFF. See [Export bit depth](/export/bit-depth/). | 16-bit |
| **Stems:** | Also writes each track's sound as its own file. See [Audio stems](/export/stems/). | None |
| **Loudness:** | **Off**, a loudness target, or **Custom…** with a LUFS field. See [Export loudness](/export/loudness/). | Off |
| **Range:** | **Whole project**, or **In/out range** when one is set. See [Export a range](/export/range/). | Whole project |
| **Burn in timecode** | Draws the project timecode into the exported picture. See [Burn in timecode](/export/burn-in-timecode/). | Off |

Every export's sound goes through a master limiter, whatever you choose here. See [Export loudness](/export/loudness/).

## Unavailable controls

A control the chosen format can't use is greyed out rather than hidden, and its value isn't sent. So a greyed-out control never affects the file.

| Control | Available on |
| --- | --- |
| **Dynamic Range:** | HEVC 10-bit (MP4), AV1 (MP4), AV1 (WebM), VP9 (WebM), ProRes 422 (MOV) and ProRes 4444 (MOV). On any other format it's greyed out and shows **SDR version**, which is what that format writes. |
| **Speed:** | AV1 (MP4) and AV1 (WebM) |
| **Size:**, **Frame rate:** and **Burn in timecode** | Every format but the three audio-only ones |
| **Quality:** | Every format but ProRes, WAV, AIFF, GIF and APNG |
| **Bit depth:** | Audio only (WAV) and Audio only (AIFF) |
| **Stems:** | The three audio-only formats |
| **Loudness:** | Every format but GIF and APNG |

**Speed:**, **Bit depth:** and **Stems:** go on showing your last choice while they're greyed out, and it comes back when you pick a format that uses it.

**Range:** doesn't depend on the format. It's greyed out when the project has no in/out range. It's greyed out inside a nest too, even when the nest has a range, and its tooltip says why: an export writes the whole timeline, so it can't use a range that belongs to the nest. Leave the nest with <kbd>⌘↑</kbd> and set a range on the timeline.

## The readout line

The line under the controls says what size, rate and length the file will have. These are the file's real numbers, so a GIF's fitted size or an evened edge shows here.

| Kind of file | The readout looks like |
| --- | --- |
| A movie | `1920 × 1080 · 30 fps · 00:01:12:05` |
| An audio-only file | `Audio only · 00:01:12.200` |
| A GIF or APNG | The movie line, followed by `· 360 frames, no audio` |

When the sheet can't work out a valid file, the readout says what to fix and **Export…** and **Add to Queue** are greyed out. An empty custom field gives "Type a width and a height, or pick a size from the list." or "Type a loudness target in LUFS, or pick one from the list."

## Estimated time

On AV1 (MP4), AV1 (WebM), VP9 (WebM) and VP9 with Alpha (WebM) a second line estimates how long the export will take, for example `Estimated time: about 25 s`. The other formats show no estimate.

| How long | It reads |
| --- | --- |
| Under a minute | Seconds, in steps of 5: `about 25 s` |
| Under an hour | Whole minutes: `about 3 min` |
| An hour or more | `about 1 h 5 min` |

The estimate follows the format, **Speed:**, the size, the frame rate and the range.

It's only an estimate. The figures behind it are the median of three measured exports per format at 1080p and 4K, of real 4K camera footage on an idle Apple M2 Max. On exports it wasn't fitted on, 30 seconds at 2560 × 1440, it came within 14 % of the real time. A slower Mac, a busy one or a heavy timeline takes longer.

## The footnote

The small line under the readout names what the file is made of. It lists these in order, leaving out whatever doesn't apply:

1. The codec, such as `H264`, `AV1` or `PRORES422`.
2. The container, unless it's the same word as the codec, as in `GIF`.
3. The AV1 speed, such as `Balanced`.
4. `24-bit` for a 24-bit WAV or AIFF.
5. The number of stems, such as `3 stems`.
6. The video rate, when you've picked a Quality tier. AV1 and VP9 rates read `usually ≤ …`, because the rate is a [soft cap](/export/av1-and-vp9/#the-rate-as-a-soft-cap).
7. The audio rate, when you've picked a Quality tier, such as `192 kbps audio`.
8. The loudness target, such as `−14 LUFS`.
9. `alpha`, when the format keeps transparency.

So a plain export reads `H264 · MP4`, an AV1 file `AV1 · MP4 · Balanced` or `AV1 · WEBM · Balanced`, and a transparent web movie `VP9 · WEBM · alpha`. With High quality and a loudness target at 1080p and 30 fps, an H.264 file reads `H264 · MP4 · 8.0 Mbps · 256 kbps audio · −14 LUFS`.

## The remembered choice

The sheet reopens on the last choices you exported with. Choosing **Export…** or **Add to Queue** records them, and **Cancel** doesn't. With nothing remembered, it opens on H.264 at the document's own size.

The remembered choice belongs to the app, not the project, so every document's sheet opens on it.

- Only what the format could use is remembered. After a WAV, for example, there's no size or frame rate to bring back.
- A remembered size row that the format doesn't list falls back to a row with the same numbers, or else to the format's default.
- A remembered **In/out range** falls back to **Whole project** on a document with no range.
- **Dynamic Range:** isn't remembered. It opens on **HDR (HLG)** every time.

To keep a set of choices under a name, save an [export preset](/export/presets/).

## Export or Add to Queue

The sheet ends in three buttons.

| Button | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Cancel** | Closes the sheet. Nothing is written and nothing is remembered. |
| **Export…** | Opens a save panel, then writes the file behind a [progress sheet](/export/progress-and-report/). It doesn't join the queue and never waits for memory. |
| **Add to Queue** | Opens the same save panel, then puts the job in the [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/). The job keeps the project as it is now, and you can go on editing. |

**Export…** and **Add to Queue** are greyed out while the sheet can't work out a valid file, for example with an empty custom field, or when the file would have no length.

The save panel suggests the project's name with the format's extension, such as `Board v1.2.mp4`. Its message says what's being written: "Export the timeline as a movie.", "Export the timeline as an animated GIF." or "Export the timeline's audio."

## Good to know

- An audio-only format on a timeline with no sound stops after the save panel with "There is nothing on the timeline to export — add a clip first."
- A custom size of a different shape from the canvas passes the readout, but the formats that keep transparency stop on it after the save panel. See [Transparent exports](/export/transparency/).

## With an agent

`export` starts the job and answers at once. Every agent export goes through the [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/), never behind a progress sheet. It takes the sheet's choices but not **Frame rate:**, so it writes the document's rate, or GIF's and APNG's own. It can also set a ceiling for the master limiter other than the sheet's fixed one, and it replaces an existing file at its path. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/).

The **Format:** popup in the [export sheet](/export/export-sheet/) decides the codec and the container together. Pick it by where the file is going next.

<AtAGlance
  where="Export sheet ▸ Format"
  tools="export"
/>

## Pick by what the file is for

| You want | Choose |
| --- | --- |
| A file every player and upload form takes | [H.264 (MP4)](/export/h264-and-hevc/#h264-mp4), the default |
| A smaller file at the same picture | [HEVC (MP4)](/export/h264-and-hevc/#hevc-mp4) |
| The smallest delivery file, and time to spare | [AV1 (MP4)](/export/av1-and-vp9/#av1-mp4) |
| To keep a 10-bit source's gradients in a delivery file | [HEVC 10-bit (MP4)](/export/h264-and-hevc/#hevc-10-bit-mp4) |
| A movie for a web page | [VP9 (WebM)](/export/av1-and-vp9/#vp9-webm) or [AV1 (WebM)](/export/av1-and-vp9/#av1-webm) |
| A master for another editing application | [ProRes 422 (MOV)](/export/prores/#prores-422-mov) |
| A title or lower third with transparency | [ProRes 4444 (MOV)](/export/prores/#prores-4444-mov) as a master, [HEVC with Alpha (MOV)](/export/h264-and-hevc/#hevc-with-alpha-mov) for Safari and Apple's apps, or [VP9 with Alpha (WebM)](/export/av1-and-vp9/#vp9-with-alpha-webm) for Chrome and Firefox |
| Sound and no picture | [An audio-only format](/export/audio-only/) |
| A short silent loop | [Animated GIF or Animated PNG](/export/gif-and-apng/) |

## The formats

They're listed in the popup's order.

| Format | What it's for | File | Sound | Picture depth | Keeps transparency | Can carry HDR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H.264 (MP4) | The everyday delivery file | `.mp4` | AAC | 8-bit | No | No |
| HEVC (MP4) | A smaller file at the same picture | `.mp4` | AAC | 8-bit | No | No |
| HEVC with Alpha (MOV) | A small transparent delivery file | `.mov` | AAC | 8-bit | Yes | No |
| HEVC 10-bit (MP4) | Keeps a 10-bit source's gradients | `.mp4` | AAC | 10-bit | No | Yes |
| AV1 (MP4) | The smallest delivery file | `.mp4` | AAC | 10-bit | No | Yes |
| AV1 (WebM) | The same AV1 picture, for the web | `.webm` | Opus | 10-bit | No | Yes |
| VP9 (WebM) | The web format every browser plays | `.webm` | Opus | 8-bit, or 10-bit when it carries HDR | No | Yes |
| VP9 with Alpha (WebM) | A transparent movie for Chrome and Firefox | `.webm` | Opus | 8-bit | Yes | No |
| ProRes 422 (MOV) | An editing master for another application | `.mov` | 16-bit LPCM | 10-bit | No | Yes |
| ProRes 4444 (MOV) | A master that keeps transparency | `.mov` | 16-bit LPCM | 12-bit | Yes | Yes |
| Audio only (M4A) | Compressed sound to send | `.m4a` | AAC | None | None | None |
| Audio only (WAV) | Uncompressed sound for another tool | `.wav` | 16-bit or 24-bit LPCM | None | None | None |
| Audio only (AIFF) | The same samples as WAV, in an AIFF | `.aiff` | 16-bit or 24-bit LPCM | None | None | None |
| Animated GIF | A short silent loop to send | `.gif` | None | 8-bit, 256 colours | No | No |
| Animated PNG | A lossless silent loop | `.png` | None | 8-bit | Yes | No |

In an HDR project, a video format that can't carry HDR writes the project's SDR version. See [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/). On a transparent canvas, a format that doesn't keep transparency composites the picture onto black, and a GIF has a rule of its own. See [Transparent exports](/export/transparency/).

## Sound in each format

Every file with sound is stereo at 48 kHz.

| Sound | Formats |
| --- | --- |
| AAC | H.264, HEVC, HEVC with Alpha, HEVC 10-bit, AV1 (MP4) and M4A |
| Opus | AV1 (WebM), VP9 (WebM) and VP9 with Alpha (WebM) |
| 16-bit LPCM | ProRes 422 and ProRes 4444 |
| 16-bit or 24-bit LPCM | WAV and AIFF. See [Export bit depth](/export/bit-depth/). |
| None | GIF and APNG |

AAC and Opus run at 192 kbps unless a [Quality tier](/export/quality/) says otherwise.

A file's sound is as long as the range it exports, including when a clip in it plays faster or slower. A project with no sound exports a movie with no sound track, in a WebM as in any other movie format.

## Changing the format

Changing the format rebuilds the **Size:** list and returns it to that format's default, because a GIF's default isn't an H.264's. Your frame rate, quality, loudness and range choices stay as they were, whether or not the new format can use them.

Picking the format that's already chosen changes nothing, so a custom size you've typed survives it.

## Software and hardware encoders

AV1 and VP9 are encoded in software, by encoders built into Frame Job, so they take longer than the HEVC formats, which use the Mac's hardware encoder. The sheet [estimates the time](/export/export-sheet/#estimated-time) for AV1 and VP9, and AV1's [**Speed:** row](/export/encoder-speed/) trades time against file size.

## No encoder

A Mac with no encoder for a format reports it and leaves no file. The message names the format by its short name, for example: "This Mac cannot export with the “hevc_alpha” preset."

title: "H.264 and HEVC"
description: "Know what the H.264, HEVC, HEVC 10-bit and HEVC with Alpha formats write, and which one suits your delivery file."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

These four formats are for delivery. H.264 is the file everything takes, HEVC is smaller, HEVC 10-bit keeps a deep source's gradients, and HEVC with Alpha keeps a transparent canvas.

<AtAGlance
  where="Export sheet ▸ Format"
  tools="export"
/>

| Format | File | Picture | Keeps transparency | In an HDR project | Rate at 1080p, 30 fps with Format default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [H.264 (MP4)](#h264-mp4) | `.mp4` | 8-bit | No | Writes the SDR version | About 8.7 Mbps |
| [HEVC (MP4)](#hevc-mp4) | `.mp4` | 8-bit | No | Writes the SDR version | About 4.4 Mbps |
| [HEVC 10-bit (MP4)](#hevc-10-bit-mp4) | `.mp4` | 10-bit | No | Writes HDR | About 4.4 Mbps |
| [HEVC with Alpha (MOV)](#hevc-with-alpha-mov) | `.mov` | 8-bit | Yes | Writes the SDR version | About 4.4 Mbps |

All four share these:

- A keyframe at least every 2 seconds, so the file scrubs and re-cuts well.
- AAC sound, stereo at 48 kHz, at 192 kbps unless a [Quality tier](/export/quality/) says otherwise.
- Even dimensions. An odd width or height is written one pixel smaller. See [Export size](/export/size/).
- [Chapters](/export/chapters/) from your chapter markers.

## H.264 (MP4)

This is the default, the first row of the **Format:** popup, so <kbd>⌘E</kbd> writes it unless you've chosen otherwise. Every player and upload form takes it.

It writes 8-bit video in the High profile. With **Format default**, the rate follows the frame at 0.14 bits per pixel per frame, held between 1 and 200 Mbps.

H.264 has no alpha channel, so a transparent canvas is flattened onto black.

## HEVC (MP4)

HEVC gives you the same picture in about half the rate of H.264, though not everything accepts it yet. It uses the Mac's hardware encoder.

It writes 8-bit video in the Main profile, even from a deep source. With **Format default**, the rate is 0.07 bits per pixel per frame, held between 1 and 200 Mbps. The Quality tiers ask for 60 % of H.264's rate.

## HEVC 10-bit (MP4)

HEVC 10-bit writes HEVC's Main 10 profile from Frame Job's deep frames, so a 10-bit source keeps its gradients in a delivery file. Its rates are HEVC's.

It's one of the six formats that can carry HDR. In an HLG project it writes HLG unless you change **Dynamic Range:**, and no Dolby Vision is added to the file. See [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/).

## HEVC with Alpha (MOV)

This is a small delivery movie that keeps a transparent canvas, for laying over another background. It's the transparent movie for Safari, QuickTime and Apple's apps. For a web page in Chrome or Firefox, see [VP9 with Alpha (WebM)](/export/av1-and-vp9/#vp9-with-alpha-webm), and for a master, [ProRes 4444 (MOV)](/export/prores/#prores-4444-mov).

- It's a `.mov` because this codec can't be written into an `.mp4`.
- The picture and its alpha are both 8-bit, and the colour is straight, not multiplied by the transparency.
- It takes HEVC's rates and Quality tiers, and the [footnote](/export/export-sheet/#the-footnote) ends in `alpha`.
- [Fast start](#fast-start) is off.

Every row in the **Size:** popup has the canvas's shape, so those are all fine. A **Custom…** size of a different shape won't export, because padding it would lose the alpha. After the save panel the export stops with a message naming the canvas's size. A size within a pixel of the canvas's shape, or in the same proportions at any scale, is fine.

## Fast start

MP4 and M4A files are written with their index at the front, so a player can start before the whole file has downloaded. There's no control for this in the sheet.

Fast start is on for MP4 and M4A, and off for MOV, WAV, AIFF, GIF and APNG. A WebM's index is at the front anyway.

## Good to know

H.264, HEVC and HEVC with Alpha are all 8-bit, so in an HDR project they write the project's SDR version and **Dynamic Range:** stays greyed out on **SDR version**. To deliver HDR in this family, use HEVC 10-bit.

title: "ProRes"
description: "Export a ProRes 422 or ProRes 4444 master for another application, and see what each one keeps."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

ProRes files are masters: their next reader is another application, not a viewer. ProRes 422 is the one to reach for first. ProRes 4444 is larger, and you choose it when you need the alpha channel.

<AtAGlance
  where="Export sheet ▸ Format"
  tools="export"
/>

| | ProRes 422 (MOV) | ProRes 4444 (MOV) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Picture | 10-bit | 12-bit |
| Keeps transparency | No | Yes |
| Odd width or height | Written one pixel smaller | Kept |
| A custom size of a different shape | Letterboxed with black | Won't export |

Both are `.mov` files with these in common:

- The data rate is fixed by the profile, so **Quality:** is greyed out.
- The sound is 16-bit, 48 kHz stereo LPCM. **Bit depth:** is greyed out, because 24-bit is for WAV and AIFF.
- Both can carry HDR. In an HLG project they write HLG unless you change **Dynamic Range:**. See [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/).
- [Chapters](/export/chapters/) are written.
- [Fast start](/export/h264-and-hevc/#fast-start) is off, because an editing master has no need of it.

## ProRes 422 (MOV)

Use this as an editing master for another application. It keeps 10 bits of Frame Job's deep frames.

ProRes 422 has no alpha channel, so a transparent canvas is flattened onto black.

## ProRes 4444 (MOV)

Use this for a title, a lower third or anything else another application will composite over its own footage. It keeps 12 bits and the alpha channel, and the [footnote](/export/export-sheet/#the-footnote) ends in `alpha`. The colour is straight, not multiplied by the transparency, so a re-imported file composites to the right colour.

It's the only movie format that keeps an odd width or height.

A **Custom…** size of a different shape from the canvas won't export, because padding would lose the alpha. After the save panel the export stops with a message naming the canvas's size. Every row in the **Size:** popup has the canvas's shape, and any custom size in the same proportions is fine.

---
title: "AV1 and VP9"
description: "Export small delivery files and web movies with Frame Job's built-in AV1 and VP9 encoders, and know how their rates, time and memory behave."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

AV1 and VP9 are the formats for the smallest delivery files and for the web. Frame Job has their encoders built in, SVT-AV1 and libvpx, and they run in software, so they take longer than HEVC.

<AtAGlance
  where={['Export sheet ▸ Format', 'Export sheet ▸ Speed (AV1 only)']}
  tools="export"
/>

| Format | File | Sound | Picture | Keeps transparency | Can carry HDR | **Speed:** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [AV1 (MP4)](#av1-mp4) | `.mp4` | AAC | 10-bit | No | Yes | Yes |
| [AV1 (WebM)](#av1-webm) | `.webm` | Opus | 10-bit | No | Yes | Yes |
| [VP9 (WebM)](#vp9-webm) | `.webm` | Opus | 8-bit, or 10-bit with HDR | No | Yes | Greyed out |
| [VP9 with Alpha (WebM)](#vp9-with-alpha-webm) | `.webm` | Opus | 8-bit | Yes | No | Greyed out |

All four write a keyframe at least every 2 seconds and need even dimensions, so an odd width or height is written one pixel smaller. All four write [chapters](/export/chapters/). The sheet [estimates the time](/export/export-sheet/#estimated-time) before you start.

## AV1 (MP4)

This is the smallest delivery file: AV1 video and AAC sound in an MP4. It's always 10-bit.

**Speed:** offers **Faster**, **Balanced** and **Smaller file**, with **Balanced** the default. See [Encoder speed](/export/encoder-speed/). Slower settings take longer and write a smaller file.

It encodes at a constant quality matched to HEVC, with the rate as a [soft cap](#the-rate-as-a-soft-cap). It's one of the six formats that can carry HDR. See [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/).

An M1 or M2 Mac can't [play the file back](#playback-on-m1-and-m2-macs).

## AV1 (WebM)

The same AV1 picture in a WebM file, for the web. It has the same encoder, speeds, soft cap and HDR as AV1 (MP4). Only the container and the sound differ.

The sound is Opus, 48 kHz stereo, at 192 kbps unless a [Quality tier](/export/quality/) says otherwise, and it snaps to the nearest rate the encoder offers. A project with no sound exports a WebM with no sound track.

## VP9 (WebM)

VP9 in a WebM file with Opus sound: the web format every browser plays. It's larger than AV1 for the same picture and slower to export than HEVC. It has one speed, so **Speed:** is greyed out.

An SDR picture is 8-bit, in VP9's Profile 0, which every player decodes. HDR is 10-bit, in Profile 2. VP9 can't name HLG or PQ itself, so the WebM file tells the player which one it is. See [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/).

## VP9 with Alpha (WebM)

VP9 (WebM) that keeps a transparent canvas, for a title or lower third a web page plays over its own background in Chrome or Firefox. It's a Safari-free choice: Safari hasn't been confirmed to show its transparency, and Safari's transparent movie is [HEVC with Alpha (MOV)](/export/h264-and-hevc/#hevc-with-alpha-mov). Only a player that decodes VP9 with libvpx shows the transparency, and others show the picture opaque.

- The picture is 8-bit, with the transparency as a second stream beside it. The [footnote](/export/export-sheet/#the-footnote) ends in `alpha`.
- It's SDR only, so an HDR project writes its SDR version, and **Dynamic Range:** stays greyed out on **SDR version**.
- The sound is Opus, as in VP9 (WebM).
- A **Custom…** size of a different shape from the canvas won't export, because padding would lose the alpha. After the save panel the export stops with a message naming the canvas's size. Every row in the **Size:** popup is fine.
- Imported back into Frame Job it shows opaque, with black where it was transparent. For a transparent clip to bring back in, export ProRes 4444 or HEVC with Alpha.

## The rate as a soft cap

On AV1 and VP9 the video rate isn't a target. They encode at a constant quality chosen to match or beat HEVC at that rate, and the file usually stays under it. That's why the Quality tiers and the footnote read `usually ≤ …`.

- With **Format default** the cap is HEVC's rate. With a tier it's 60 % of the H.264 rate, as for HEVC. See [Export quality](/export/quality/).
- Simple footage comes out much smaller than the rate.
- Very detailed footage can go over it: up to about 1.25 times on AV1, and about 1.15 times on VP9.
- In an HDR export, VP9 matches HEVC 10-bit at that rate.
- You can't know the file size in advance.

On VP9 with Alpha the rate is the picture's alone. The transparency is a second stream at a fixed quality on top of it, so the file is larger than the rate says. On a moving soft-edged shape, the transparency measured about 6 to 15 % of the video at 1080p, 9 to 21 % at 720p, and 21 to 39 % at 640 × 360, with the higher figures at the Low tier.

## Memory and the queue

These encoders use far more memory than the Mac's own. A job in the [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) waits while the AV1 and VP9 exports already running would use more than a quarter of the Mac's memory with it. Its row says why, for example "Waiting for memory: AV1 and VP9 exports running now hold about 6.0 GB of the 8.0 GB this Mac allows them, and this one needs about 3.0 GB." A later job may run first meanwhile.

A job always starts when no other AV1 or VP9 export is running. **Export…** never waits, so starting several at once behind their progress sheets can go past that quarter. The memory each job needs is a measured figure, not a guarantee, and a heavier timeline can use more.

## Playback on M1 and M2 Macs

M1 and M2 Macs have no AV1 decoder, so neither Frame Job nor QuickTime can play or re-import an AV1 file there, MP4 or WebM. The Mac can still export one.

A VP9 (WebM) file re-imports on any Apple silicon Mac.

## Good to know

An AV1 rate is held at 100 Mbps at most, whatever a tier works out to at a very large size.

## Related

- [Encoder speed](/export/encoder-speed/)
- [Export quality](/export/quality/)
- [Transparent exports](/export/transparency/)
- [The Export Queue](/export/export-queue/)

---
title: "Animated GIF and PNG"
description: "Export a short silent loop as an Animated GIF or Animated PNG, and keep it inside the size and the 600-frame limit."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

GIF and APNG are for short silent loops you can send or drop into a page. Each stores every frame as a whole picture, so a long or large one quickly becomes a file nobody can send. That's why both start small and hold at most 600 frames.

<AtAGlance
  where="Export sheet ▸ Format"
  tools="export"
/>

## Export a loop

<Steps>

1. Set an [in/out range](/timeline/in-out-range/) around the moment you want.

2. Press <kbd>⌘E</kbd>, and choose **Animated GIF** or **Animated PNG** from **Format:**.

3. Set **Range:** to **In/out range**.

4. Check the readout, which shows the size and the frame count, such as `· 360 frames, no audio`.

5. Choose **Export…**.

</Steps>

## Animated GIF

A GIF is a short, silent `.gif` that loops forever. It starts at 480 × 270 and 12.5 fps, and you can still change the size and the rate.

The 12.5 is deliberate. A GIF stores each frame's delay in hundredths of a second, so only rates that divide 100 play back exactly. 25 and 50 fps from the **Frame rate:** popup do too, and any other rate lands wherever the format's rounding puts it.

A GIF has a palette of 256 colours. It can show a pixel as fully transparent but has no partial transparency, so soft edges go hard, and it isn't one of the [formats that keep transparency](/export/transparency/).

## Animated PNG

An APNG is a lossless, silent, true-colour `.png` that loops forever. It starts at 960 × 540 and 25 fps, and you can still change the size and the rate.

It keeps real transparency, so a pixel can be any fraction of opaque, and the [footnote](/export/export-sheet/#the-footnote) ends in `alpha`. It's written at 8 bits a component and labelled BT.709.

A viewer that knows nothing of APNG shows the first frame.

## The 600-frame limit

An animated GIF or APNG holds at most 600 frames. That's 48 seconds at GIF's 12.5 fps, or 24 seconds at APNG's 25 fps. The readout shows the count while you're choosing, but the sheet doesn't stop you. Once you've picked where to save, a longer export stops before it writes anything:

> An animated GIF is limited to 600 frames and this range is 720. Shorten the range, or lower the export frame rate.

For GIF the way out is a shorter range, because every fixed rate in the **Frame rate:** popup is higher than 12.5 fps. An APNG can go down to 24 or 23.976 fps, which gains you about a second.

## Fitting inside the size

The **Size:** popup lists **GIF default** or **APNG default** first, and it's the default for those two formats and no others. Each is 480 × 270 or 960 × 540, fitted to the canvas's shape.

Every row, and a **Custom…** size, is a box the picture fits inside. It keeps its shape and is never enlarged, and nothing is letterboxed. The rows show the size the file will have. A 1080 × 1920 project's GIF default is 152 × 270.

Because the picture is never enlarged, rows bigger than the canvas come out as the canvas's own size, and the popup hides rows that repeat an earlier row's numbers. An odd width or height is kept.

## Good to know

- **Quality:** and **Loudness:** are greyed out, and so are **Bit depth:** and **Stems:**. Neither format has a bit rate or any sound.
- **Burn in timecode** still works.
- Neither format has [chapters](/export/chapters/).
- Both write the SDR version in an HDR project.

## Related

- [Choose a format](/export/formats/)
- [Export a range](/export/range/)
- [Export size](/export/size/)
- [Export frame rate](/export/frame-rate/)
